title: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
summary: Why raw clicks are biased labels, how click models (PBM, cascade, UBM, DBN) describe examination, and how inverse propensity scoring, clipping and propensity estimation turn clicks into unbiased training data.
outcomes: Explain why click-through rate confounds position with relevance and why naive training repeats the old ranking
Compare the position-based, cascade, UBM and DBN click models and what drives examination in each
Compute IPS-weighted relevance estimates from a click log and show why they are unbiased
Quantify the variance from small propensities and choose a clipping threshold as a bias-variance tradeoff
Choose a propensity estimation method: swaps, RandPair, regression EM, intervention harvesting or DLA

lessons.title: Why raw clicks teach a ranker to repeat itself

blocks.md:
You know how to train a ranker such as LambdaMART from graded relevance labels. Human labels are expensive, so every search team wants to use the free signal in its logs: **clicks**. A click looks like a vote for relevance.

The trouble is that a user can only click what they actually look at, and people look at the top of a result page far more than the bottom. This course shows how to correct for that, with every number computed by a fixed-seed simulation.

Our toy search engine has one query and five documents. The production ranker always shows them in the order **A, B, C, D, E** (rank 1 to rank 5). Each document has a hidden **relevance** $\gamma_d$: the probability that a user clicks it *if they look at it*.

- A 0.30, B 0.45, C 0.20, D 0.70, E 0.55

So the truly best order is D, E, B, A, C. The production ranker got it badly wrong: the best document sits at rank 4.

Users **examine** (look at) rank $k$ with probability $\theta_k$, independent of what is shown there. We use $\theta_k = 1/k$, the same family $(1/k)^\eta$ with $\eta = 1$ that Joachims, Swaminathan and Schnabel used to simulate position bias. So rank 1 is always seen, rank 5 only one time in five. A click happens only if the result is examined **and** the user finds it attractive.

blocks.title: Five logged sessions: what was seen and clicked

scenes.caption: Each row is one user session on the ranking A, B, C, D, E (columns are ranks 1 to 5). The log only records clicks; what the user looked at is hidden.
The hidden examination events from our simulation. Rank 1 is always seen. Session 1 skipped ranks 2 and 3 but glanced at rank 4: under this model each rank is examined independently.
Clicks happen only on examined results the user liked. Session 3 clicked B and C and session 5 clicked E. Sessions 1, 2 and 4 clicked nothing at all.
Session 1 looked at D (the best document) and did not click. Without knowing what was examined, an unclicked D looks exactly like an unexamined D.

blocks.prompt: Over 5,000 simulated sessions, which document collects the most clicks?
blocks.reveal: **A**, with 1478 clicks, even though its relevance is only 0.30. D, the most relevant document, gets 846 clicks because only about a quarter of users ever see rank 4. Expected click-through rate is $\theta_k \gamma_d$: 0.30 for A but $0.25 \times 0.70 = 0.175$ for D.

scenes.caption: Hidden truth: the probability each document is clicked once examined. D is best, then E, B, A, C.
Examination probability of the rank each document sits at: 1/k. This factor has nothing to do with the document.
Observed click-through rate (CTR) from 5,000 sessions: 0.296, 0.213, 0.071, 0.169, 0.111. Sorting by CTR gives A, B, D, E, C, almost the production order.

blocks.md: Now imagine training the next ranker with clicks as labels. A has the highest click rate, so the new model learns to keep A on top; D stays low, keeps getting few clicks, and the next round of training confirms the mistake. Joachims et al. call this distortion **presentation bias**; the dominant part of it, caused by rank alone, is **position bias**.

A low CTR at rank 4 does not mean a document is less relevant than one at rank 1. CTR mixes two things: how often the slot is seen and how good the document is. You must separate them before clicks can serve as relevance labels.

Under position bias, $P(\text{click}) = P(\text{examined at rank } k) \times P(\text{click} \mid \text{examined})$. Clicks are biased labels because the first factor depends on the old ranking, not on the document.

blocks.question: Your logs show document X at rank 1 with CTR 0.20 and document Y at rank 5 with CTR 0.08. Under our model with $\theta_k = 1/k$, which is more relevant?
options: X, because its CTR is 2.5 times higher
Y: its relevance is 0.08 / 0.2 = 0.40, double X's 0.20
They are equally relevant; CTR differences are noise
It cannot be decided without human labels
blocks.explain: Divide CTR by the examination probability of the slot: X is 0.20 / 1 = 0.20 and Y is 0.08 / 0.2 = 0.40. Y wins. This is exactly the correction the rest of the course builds.

blocks.question: A team retrains its ranker every week on raw clicks from the previous week. What is the most likely long-run effect?
options: Rankings converge to true relevance because errors average out
The ranker drifts toward random order
The ranker keeps reinforcing whatever it already put on top
Click volume rises because users see better results
blocks.explain: Documents at the top get more clicks simply because they are seen more, so the labels favor the current order and the retrained model keeps it. Averaging more biased data does not remove a systematic bias.

lessons.title: Click models: PBM, cascade, UBM and DBN

blocks.md: A **click model** is a probabilistic model of how a user scans a result page and decides what to click. Chuklin, Markov and de Rijke's book *Click Models for Web Search* traces the term to Craswell et al. (2008), who introduced the cascade model. Almost every click model is built on the **examination hypothesis**: a user clicks a document if and only if they examined it and were attracted by it.

blocks.tex: C_d = 1 \iff E_d = 1 \text{ and } A_d = 1, \qquad P(C_d = 1) = P(E_d = 1)\,P(A_d = 1)
blocks.caption: The examination hypothesis, with examination and attraction treated as independent.

blocks.md: Models differ in what drives examination. In the **position-based model (PBM)**, examination depends only on the rank: $P(E = 1) = \theta_k$, and attraction is a per query-document parameter $\gamma_{q,d}$. The book points out that attraction is a property of the snippet the user sees, which correlates with judged relevance but is not identical to it. Our toy engine from lesson 1 is exactly a PBM.

blocks.title: What drives a click in each model

scenes.caption: Position-based model: rank alone sets the chance of examination, the query-document pair sets attraction, and a click needs both.
Cascade model: the user reads top to bottom and stops at the first click. Rank k is examined only if every result above it was examined and skipped.
User browsing model (Dupret and Piwowarski, 2008): examination depends on the rank and on the rank of the most recent click above it.
DBN (Chapelle and Zhang, 2009): after a click the user may be satisfied (probability sigma) and stop; otherwise they continue down the page with a fixed probability.

blocks.md: The **cascade model** (Craswell et al., 2008) assumes the user scans from the top, examines each result in turn, and leaves after the first click. Rank 1 is always examined; rank $k$ is examined only if rank $k-1$ was examined and not clicked. So the examination probability of a slot is the product of the non-click probabilities of everything above it.

blocks.caption: Cascade examination probability for a ranking d_1, d_2, ... (a session has at most one click).

blocks.title: Cascade examination depends on what is above

scenes.caption: Cascade model on the production order A, B, C, D, E with our relevances. Rank 2 is seen with probability 1 - 0.30 = 0.700, rank 4 with 0.7 x 0.55 x 0.8 = 0.308.
Put the best documents on top (D, E, B, A, C). Now rank 2 is seen only 30 percent of the time, because 70 percent of users click D and leave.

blocks.md: That is the key difference from PBM: under the cascade model the chance that rank 2 is seen depends on which document sits at rank 1. The book also notes the practical upside: because a cascade session has at most one click, every result above the click was examined and every result below it was not, so parameters can be estimated by simple counting. The downside is that it cannot explain sessions with two or more clicks, and our PBM log has 1,005 of them in 5,000 sessions.

Later models mix the two ideas:

- **DCM** (Guo et al.) lets the user continue after a click with a rank-dependent probability.
- **UBM** keeps position-based examination but conditions it on the rank of the previous click.
- **DBN** separates *attractiveness* (the snippet earns the click) from *satisfaction* $\sigma$ (the page answered the need). A satisfied user stops; otherwise they continue with a fixed probability, written $\gamma$ in the book, which is unrelated to our relevance $\gamma_d$. **Simplified DBN** sets that continuation probability to 1.

Classic click models were built to estimate a relevance value for each query-document pair from many repeated sessions. Unbiased learning to rank borrows only the examination part, the **propensity**, and uses it to reweight individual clicks, so queries do not need to repeat.

blocks.question: A log has many sessions where users clicked results at both rank 2 and rank 5. Which model assigns these sessions zero probability?
options: The cascade model
The position-based model
The user browsing model
The dynamic Bayesian network model
blocks.explain: The cascade model ends a session at the first click, so two clicks are impossible. PBM treats ranks independently, UBM explicitly conditions on the last click, and DBN continues after an unsatisfying click.

blocks.question: Under the cascade model with the production order A, B, C, D, E, you move a highly attractive document into rank 1. What happens to the examination probability of rank 3?
options: It rises, because users trust a good top result
It stays the same, because it is a property of rank 3
It falls, because more users click at rank 1 and stop
It becomes exactly zero
blocks.explain: Cascade examination at rank 3 is (1 - gamma at rank 1)(1 - gamma at rank 2). A more attractive rank-1 document shrinks the first factor, so fewer users ever reach rank 3. It stays above zero unless gamma at rank 1 equals 1.

lessons.title: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels

blocks.md: The **propensity** of a click is the probability that the user observed that result's relevance at all. Under the PBM it is just the examination probability $\theta_k$ of the rank where the result was shown. Joachims, Swaminathan and Schnabel (WSDM 2017) borrowed **inverse propensity scoring (IPS)** from causal inference: weight every click by one over its propensity.
Why does that work? Take a document shown at rank $k$. Its click $c$ is 1 with probability $\theta_k \gamma_d$. Dividing by the known $\theta_k$ cancels the bias in expectation:

blocks.caption: Valid whenever the propensity is greater than zero for every relevant document.

blocks.title: IPS estimates from the 5,000-session log
blocks.code:
theta = [1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5]
clicks = [1478, 1066, 356, 846, 557]
N = 5000
for k in range(5):
    ctr = clicks[k] / N
    ips = clicks[k] / theta[k] / N
    print(k + 1, round(ctr, 3), round(ips, 3))

scenes.caption: Exam probabilities and click counts for ranks 1 to 5 from the 5,000-session log.
Rank 1 has weight 1: the IPS estimate equals the CTR, 0.296 (truth 0.30).
Rank 2: each click counts double. 1,066 clicks become 0.426 (truth 0.45).
Rank 3: weight 3 turns a CTR of 0.071 into 0.214 (truth 0.20).
Rank 4 holds D. Weight 4 lifts a CTR of 0.169 to 0.677 (truth 0.70): D is now the best estimate.
Rank 5: weight 5 gives E 0.557 (truth 0.55). The IPS order is D, E, B, A, C, the true order.

blocks.title: Naive CTR versus IPS against the truth

scenes.caption: Naive CTR: biased toward the top slots, ranks A first.
IPS estimates: 0.296, 0.426, 0.214, 0.677, 0.557. Each is within 0.03 of the truth, and the order D, E, B, A, C is now correct.
The hidden truth for comparison. IPS recovered it from biased clicks plus known propensities, with no human labels.

blocks.md: Joachims et al. apply this to a ranking metric, not just per-document scores. With binary relevance, take the metric $\Delta$ = sum of the ranks of the relevant documents (lower is better). For a new ranking $S$, the IPS estimate from one logged query uses only the clicked documents:

blocks.caption: rank(d|S) is the rank in the candidate ranking; the propensity uses the rank in the logged ranking y-bar.

blocks.prompt: A logged session shows A, B, C, D, E and the user clicked A (rank 1) and D (rank 4), with propensities 1 and 0.25. Score the old ranking and a new one that swaps A and D. Which does IPS prefer, and what would an unweighted sum say?
blocks.reveal: Old ranking: $1/1 + 4/0.25 = 17$. New ranking (D at 1, A at 4): $1/0.25 + 4/1 = 8$. IPS prefers the new ranking. The unweighted sum is $1 + 4 = 5$ for both, a tie: without weights, the click on a rarely seen rank-4 result counts no more than the click on rank 1.

blocks.md: Because each query instance gives an unbiased estimate, the average over many queries is an unbiased estimate of the true risk, and you can minimize it. Their **Propensity SVM-Rank** turns each clicked result into a training example with weight $1/q$, where $q$ is its propensity, and asks it to outrank every other candidate. Any loss built from per-click terms can be reweighted the same way; the snippet below uses a softmax cross-entropy, the loss used by the dual learning algorithm in lesson 5.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np

def ips_softmax_loss(scores, clicked, ranks, theta, tau=0.0):
    # scores: model scores for the logged list
    # clicked: 0/1 per document; ranks: 1-based logged ranks
    log_p = scores - np.log(np.sum(np.exp(scores)))
    w = 1.0 / np.maximum(theta[ranks - 1], tau)
    return -np.sum(clicked * w * log_p)
blocks.caption: Per-query IPS-weighted listwise loss. Only clicked documents contribute; tau is an optional clipping threshold (lesson 4).

blocks.md: Only clicked documents need propensities, and the estimate is unbiased only if the propensities are correct and every relevant document has a nonzero chance of being observed. Joachims et al. also require that propensities depend only on logged information (unconfoundedness).

IPS fixes the examination part of the bias, not click noise. If users sometimes click irrelevant results, those clicks are also upweighted. Joachims et al. show that, as long as relevant results are clicked more often than irrelevant ones, this bias is order preserving: with enough data the best ranking stays the same, but the estimates are no longer exactly relevance.

blocks.question: A result at logged rank 10 with propensity 0.1 is clicked once. Under IPS, how much does that click count compared with one click at rank 1 (propensity 1)?
options: The same, a click is a click
One tenth as much, because the slot is unreliable
Ten times as much
It is discarded because the propensity is below 0.2
blocks.explain: The weight is 1/0.1 = 10. Only one in ten users looked at rank 10, so each observed click stands for about ten users who would have clicked had they looked.

blocks.question: Which statement about the IPS estimator is correct?
options: It needs propensities for unclicked documents too
It is unbiased only if the same query repeats many times
It needs the logged ranking to be random
It is unbiased per query instance, so sparse queries are fine
blocks.explain: The proof works per query instance: the expectation over examination of c/theta is gamma for each instance. That is why IPS suits sparse logs like personal search, where classic per-pair click models fail. Unclicked documents contribute zero, so their propensities are not needed.

lessons.title: Small propensities, high variance, and clipping

blocks.md: Unbiased does not mean accurate. A click at rank $k$ is multiplied by $1/\theta_k$, so rare low-rank clicks get huge weights and the estimate jumps around from one log to the next. Make the bias steeper to see it: set $\theta_k = 1/k^2$ ($\eta = 2$), giving propensities 1, 0.25, 0.111, 0.0625 and 0.04. A click at rank 5 now counts **25** times.

We simulated 4,000 independent logs of $n = 500$ sessions each on the same A to E ranking, computed the IPS estimate in each, and measured the spread. The variance of one weighted click has a closed form, which matches the simulation:

blocks.caption: For D at rank 4: sqrt(0.7 x 0.956 / (0.0625 x 500)) = 0.146; the simulation gives 0.147.

blocks.title: Spread of IPS estimates across 4,000 logs

scenes.caption: Standard deviation of the IPS estimate with n = 500 sessions. Rank 1 wobbles by 0.021; D and E at ranks 4 and 5 wobble by 0.147 and 0.161, about a fifth and over a quarter of their values.
With only 100 sessions every SD grows by about sqrt(5). E's estimate now has SD 0.36. The best document D comes out on top in only 54 percent of logs (vs 75 percent at n = 500).

blocks.md: **Propensity clipping** trades bias for variance: replace each propensity by $\max(\theta_k, \tau)$ for a threshold $\tau$, so no weight exceeds $1/\tau$. Joachims et al. cite this idea from the counterfactual learning literature and show that clipping improved Propensity SVM-Rank when click data was small, with $\tau$ chosen by cross-validation. For a clipped rank the estimate now converges to $\gamma_d \theta_k / \tau$ instead of $\gamma_d$.

blocks.prompt: With $\tau = 0.0625$ only rank 5 (E, propensity 0.04) is clipped. Predict what happens to how often D is correctly ranked first, starting from 75 percent.
blocks.reveal: It rises to **94 percent**. E's estimate is shrunk toward 0.55 x 0.04 / 0.0625 = 0.35, so its wild upward swings no longer beat D. The price: E's average is now 0.35 instead of 0.55, and its RMSE rises from 0.161 to 0.225. Clipping helped the decision we cared about while making one estimate worse.

blocks.title: Mean estimate under different clipping thresholds

scenes.caption: No clipping: averaged over 4,000 logs the estimates match the truth (0.30, 0.45, 0.20, 0.70, 0.55). Unbiased, but noisy at ranks 4 and 5.
tau = 0.0625 clips only rank 5. E drops to 0.35 on average (biased), but D is now first in 94 percent of logs.
tau = 0.1 also clips rank 4. D falls to 0.438, below B at 0.451, so D is first in only 44 percent of logs. Too much clipping recreates position bias.

blocks.title: Error of one document's IPS estimate versus its propensity

scenes.caption: Unclipped error (blue) explodes as the propensity shrinks: it scales like one over the square root of theta times n. Clipping (orange) caps the variance but adds bias left of tau. Dots are the simulated values for D.
More data shrinks variance but not bias. At n = 5000 the unclipped curve wins almost everywhere: clipping pays off only when data is scarce.
With little data (n = 100) and a small tau, clipping lowers error for the rarest slots. Drag tau to find the crossover.

blocks.md: Clipping changes what the estimator measures. A clipped rank is systematically undervalued, which pushes documents shown low back down, the same direction as the original position bias. Tune $\tau$ on held-out data and report it.

Joachims et al. found misspecified propensities still beat ignoring the bias if the error is conservative: overestimating small propensities (assuming milder bias) is tolerable, underestimating them (assuming steeper bias) can hurt. Clipping is one way of overestimating small propensities.

blocks.question: A ranker trained with IPS on a small log performs erratically: retraining on a different week of logs reorders many results. Propensities at ranks 8 to 10 are around 0.02. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Drop the propensity weights and train on raw clicks
Clip propensities at a tuned tau, or collect more data
Multiply all propensities by 10
Use only clicks at ranks 8 to 10
blocks.explain: Erratic retraining points to variance from weights near 50. Clipping caps them; more data shrinks variance directly. Dropping weights reintroduces bias, and scaling all propensities by a constant does not change the ranking the estimator prefers.

blocks.question: You clip at tau = 0.2 with theta_k = 1/k. A document at rank 10 has relevance 0.6. What does its clipped estimate converge to?
blocks.explain: Expected value is gamma x theta / tau = 0.6 x 0.1 / 0.2 = 0.3. With infinite data the bias stays: the document looks half as relevant as it is.

lessons.title: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning

blocks.md: Everything so far assumed we know $\theta_k$. In practice it must be estimated, and it only needs to be known up to a constant factor, since scaling every weight does not change which ranking IPS prefers. So we estimate ratios $\theta_k / \theta_1$.

**Swap intervention** (Joachims et al.): for a small slice of traffic, swap the results at rank 1 and rank $k$. Under the PBM the same mix of documents now appears in both slots, so relevance cancels and the click ratio between the two slots estimates $\theta_k/\theta_1$. Wang et al. (SIGIR 2016) used heavier **result randomization**, uniformly shuffling the top results for a small fraction of users.

scenes.caption: For each k we simulated 2,000 sessions that swap ranks 1 and k half the time (theta_k = 1/k). Estimated ratio = clicks at rank k / clicks at rank 1.
Rank 3 is spot on (0.333). Rank 5 reads 0.165 against 0.2: only 140 clicks landed there, so the low slots are estimated from the fewest clicks.

blocks.md: Swapping a rank-10 result into rank 1 visibly hurts those users. Wang, Golbandi, Bendersky, Metzler and Najork (WSDM 2018) compared **RandTopN** (shuffle the top N) with **RandPair** (swap only adjacent ranks $k-1$ and $k$), chaining adjacent ratios: $\theta_k/\theta_1 = (\theta_2/\theta_1)(\theta_3/\theta_2)\cdots(\theta_k/\theta_{k-1})$. Both gave similar estimates in email and file search, and RandTopN degraded search quality more.

Their main proposal avoids randomization entirely: fit the PBM to ordinary logs with **expectation-maximization (EM)**. Both $\theta_k$ and $\gamma_{q,d}$ are unknown. The E-step computes, for every unclicked impression, how likely it was unexamined versus unattractive; a click means both happened:

blocks.tex: P(E=1, R=0 \mid C=0) = \frac{\theta_k (1-\gamma_{q,d})}{1 - \theta_k \gamma_{q,d}}, \qquad P(E=0, R=1 \mid C=0) = \frac{(1-\theta_k)\gamma_{q,d}}{1 - \theta_k \gamma_{q,d}}
blocks.caption: The M-step sets theta_k to the average posterior of E at rank k and gamma to the average posterior of R for that pair.

blocks.title: EM recovers position bias from two rankers' logs

scenes.caption: Log: 5,000 sessions of ranker 1 (A, B, C, D, E) and 5,000 of ranker 2 (D, E, A, B, C). Start EM with every theta and gamma at 0.5, so all ratios are 1.
After 1 iteration the ratios already decrease with rank, but the tail is too flat.
After 5 iterations rank 3 is nearly right (0.334); ranks 4 and 5 are still too high.
After 20 iterations ranks 3 and 4 are close; rank 5 (0.261 vs 0.2) is still about 30 percent high and rank 2 (0.633) is still converging.
After 1,000 iterations: 0.525, 0.333, 0.256, 0.221 against 0.5, 0.333, 0.25, 0.2. The relevances come out as 0.296, 0.423, 0.196, 0.699, 0.524 (scaled by theta_1).

blocks.md: EM can only separate rank from document if the same documents appear at different ranks, and those overlaps must link all ranks together. When ranker 2 was D, E, B, A, C instead, ranks {1, 4} and {2, 3, 5} never shared a document, the relative scale between the two groups was unidentifiable, and EM's answer for rank 2 depended on its starting point: 0.63 starting from 0.5, 0.53 starting from 0.3 (truth 0.5).

Personal search makes identifier-based EM hard: documents are private and clicks per (query, document) pair are very sparse. **Regression EM** replaces the per-pair $\gamma_{q,d}$ with a function of ranking features, $\gamma = f(x_{q,d})$, so similar documents share strength. In the M-step it samples binary relevance labels from the E-step posteriors and fits a gradient-boosted tree model (the paper used depth-3 trees with shrinkage 0.2).

Two later ideas remove the need for dedicated experiments:

- **Intervention harvesting** (Agarwal, Zaitsev, Wang, Li, Najork, Joachims, WSDM 2019): logs from several historic rankers, such as A/B test arms, already contain the same document for the same query at different ranks. Those pairs act as natural swaps, provided the query distribution does not depend on which ranker served it. An extremum estimator then combines the many local swaps into one consistent set of propensities.
- **Dual learning algorithm, DLA** (Ai, Bi, Luo, Guo, Croft, SIGIR 2018): treat propensity estimation as the mirror image of unbiased ranking. Train the ranker with inverse *propensity* weights and the propensity model with inverse *relevance* weights, updating both from the same click batches, with softmax cross-entropy losses.

blocks.title: An unbiased learning-to-rank loop in production

scenes.caption: Users click on rankings and the logs record clicks plus the rank each result was shown at.
Swap-based methods need a small intervention slice to estimate theta_k. EM, harvesting and DLA get it from regular logs.
Training reweights each click by one over its propensity (possibly clipped) and fits the next ranker, which in turn generates new logs.
DLA merges the propensity estimator and the training box: both models are learned jointly from the same clicks.

blocks.md: For experiments, the open-source [ULTRA toolbox](https://github.com/ULTR-Community/ULTRA) implements a naive click baseline, IPW, regression EM, DLA, pairwise debiasing (Unbiased LambdaMART) and online methods, with input layers that simulate clicks on ranked lists. [PyClick](https://github.com/markovi/PyClick) implements classic click models such as PBM, cascade, UBM and DBN.

Pick the propensity source by how much user disruption you can afford: randomization or swaps are simplest and most trustworthy, EM and intervention harvesting use existing logs but rest on model assumptions, and DLA learns everything jointly. Every option inherits the click model's assumptions; if users behave like a cascade, a position-only propensity is misspecified.

blocks.question: You only have logs from one fixed production ranker that never changes the order for a given query. Which method can still estimate position bias from these logs alone?
options: Intervention harvesting
Regression EM, using features shared by documents at different ranks
Identifier-based EM over (query, document) pairs
None: a swap experiment is mandatory
blocks.explain: Harvesting needs several rankers, and identifier-based EM needs each pair at multiple ranks. Regression EM only needs similar feature vectors to appear at different ranks, which happens across queries even with one deterministic ranker, though it relies on the regression model being right.

blocks.question: In a RandPair experiment that swaps ranks 3 and 4 half the time, rank 4 receives 600 clicks and rank 3 receives 800. Earlier experiments gave theta_2/theta_1 = 0.6 and theta_3/theta_2 = 0.7. What is theta_4/theta_1?
blocks.explain: Under a 50/50 swap both slots see the same document mix, so theta_4/theta_3 = 600/800 = 0.75. Chain the ratios: 0.6 x 0.7 x 0.75 = 0.315, about 0.32.
